en: Chapter on the Chan Gate, spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty.
Regarding the ancestral practice of contemplative cultivation, there are generally three types of clearly elucidated dhyāna: first, sequential; second, non-sequential; and third, responsive.

The conditions are either indeterminate or sequential and non-sequential. If they are sequential, one begins with *ānāpāna-smṛti* (counting the breath), followed by the threshold stage of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-anāgamya*), the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the six subtle gates (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-dvāra*), and the sixteen special excellences (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*).

Then follow the universal clarity (*sāmānya-prakāśa*), the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the ten notions (*daśasaṃjñā*), the eight recollections (*aṣṭānusmṛti*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the transformations (*nirmāṇa*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the nine concentrations (*navasamādhi*), the masteries (*vaśitā*), and the leap-over concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*).

One practices the various dhyānas through equal application. Next, from the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vastūni*), the four truths, and the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), there arise the various categories of the Path, the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), and the wisdom of equal application within the various dhyānas.
This continues until, beneath the Bodhi tree, one attains Buddhahood through thirty-four moments of mind while sitting cross-legged, severing delusions and becoming a Sage.
According to the teachings of the provisional method for disciples of dull faculties, these stages clarify the gradual cultivation of dhyāna.
From the shallow to the profound, each stage is distinguished individually without confusion or intermixture.

One cannot apply the name "foundations of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) to that which follows the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), nor can one place the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) before the practice of counting the breaths (ānāpānasmṛti).

To do so would contradict the sūtras and śāstras and fail to establish the proper sequence. Therefore, following the systematic thread [of the teachings], I shall distinguish their names and characteristics; thus it is called "sequential dhyāna" (anupūrva-dhyāna), not non-sequential.
This refers to those of sharp faculties who attain sudden enlightenment in the Mahāyāna—such as the assembly of those in the eight *dhyānas* gathered in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

They clarify the intrinsic nature of the nine kinds of great *dhyāna*: the *dhyāna* of all virtuous persons, the *dhyāna* of removing affliction through all practices, and the *dhyāna* of the purity of bliss in future lives.
They directly contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, transcending names and severing marks, so that mental dharmas vanish; this is beyond the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).

Examine and cleanse [the mind]. Realize that the body is fundamentally illusory. Beginning with the preliminary stages of hearing and reflection upon the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and culminating in the fruit of Great Bodhi, although there are distinctions among the nine dhyānas, all are investigations of the mind according to principle; there are no further rungs of a ladder within phenomenal affairs.

Because it follows the sequence described above, it is called "non-sequential. Having already manifested śamatha and vipaśyanā (etc.), it is a non-localized meditation that reaches sentient beings according to their capacities. This clarifies dhyāna.

This refers to that which is neither sequential nor non-sequential. There exists a distinct class of karmic conditions that possess neither the faculties for gradual expedient means nor the nature of sudden enlightenment.
For such cases, one cannot definitively formulate a teaching of sequence, nor can one definitively formulate a teaching of non-sequence.
Rather, one should respond to these karmic conditions through a boundless and indeterminate approach. This...
Because conditions are indeterminate, they cannot be standardized; therefore, it is said that they are neither sequential nor non-sequential.

These three [categories] share the same names as those commonly explained in conventional teachings—namely, the Sudden, the Gradual, the Partial, and the Indeterminate—but their intended meaning regarding the lack of fixed correspondence differs from the conventional.
If these three meanings are applied to the various teachings, then within the Tripiṭaka Teaching, there is the Abhidharma...
What is taught in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) refers to the sequential [stages of] intent.

That which is elucidated in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*—the gathering of the assembly of the eight dhyānas, clarifying that sixty billion bodhisattvas have attained the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), and the analysis of the characteristics of the meditative concentrations cultivated by the forty-two sages—this is not of the sequential intent. If it were as in the various Mahāyāna sūtras...
Regarding those who hold that there is no fixed direction or certainty, this is precisely the correct intent of the Three Treatises (Sanlun).

Those who wish to study and inquire often use wisdom to investigate and establish the names of the "Three Teachings. Now, based on the mind’s entry into the Way, we establish the names of the "Three Dhyānas.

These two perspectives are recorded in other texts. Here, we are specifically clarifying the characteristics of the shallow and deep stages of the Sequential Dhyāna Gate; therefore, it is called the "Method of Sequence."
It is a gateway. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The sequential practice and training in the Path"—this refers to this very meaning.
Question: One should speak of *prajñā*; why then do you speak of this sequential gate of dhyāna? Answer: It is for the sake of manifesting *prajñā*.
Just as *prajñā* clarifies true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), so too, for the sake of manifesting *prajñā*, one clarifies the emptiness of all other sequential dharmas. Why is this so? If now...

This does not encompass the gate of the gradual sequence from shallow to deep. One practices Prajñā later on, yet before the emptiness of Prajñā has even arisen, one mistakenly claims that other forms of emptiness have already been realized beforehand.
Now, the sequential distinctions of their differing characteristics are clarified in order to manifest Prajñā.

Furthermore, the reason for this is that since one has already discerned all phenomena (*dharma*), when practicing the untainted (*anāsrava*), tainted states may arise spontaneously without being sought.
If one does not first anticipate this and declares them to be non-Dharmas, claiming they contradict Prajñā, then the thought of rejection will arise.

If one accepts them unilaterally, one again confuses them with the works of Māra; yet if one rejects them entirely, one again deviates from Prajñā. Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish between them. Furthermore, [this applies] to those who approach...
This is due to the karmic conditions of sentient beings. If one possesses great capacity, merely hearing the Prajñāpāramitā allows them to realize its profound principle;
if one lacks such great capacity, one must necessarily rely on the "house" (the preliminary stages) to enter that principle; therefore, the sequential teaching is expounded.

Furthermore, because the inclinations and joys of sentient beings differ, they are first constrained by their desires and subsequently led into the Buddha-way. Moreover, the sequential teaching is given so that one may know the place of origin of the Prajñāpāramitā.
When practicing Prajñā, one must necessarily take a single dharma-gate as a skillful means to serve as the locus for the arising of Prajñā;
once one has attained any one dharma to harmonize the mind, one is then capable of cultivating Prajñā, and Prajñā will arise.

The reason for clarifying this sequence is that if one practices emptiness directly within the context of the five perfections, it becomes the emptiness of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), like consuming excessive salt. If there were only the five perfections [without emptiness], [the same fault would occur].
The five perfections are useless; they merely establish the dharmas of ordinary beings. Now, one cultivates emptiness through the right path to clarify prajñā.
One enters prajñā only after using the five perfections to harmonize the mind. Furthermore, the reason this sequence is taught is to adorn prajñā.
Moreover, the reason the sequence is taught is to benefit prajñā; just as fire becomes fierce when there is much fuel, so too does prajñā—which is itself a nameless dharma—shatter all dharmas.
Therefore, it is called *prajñā*. If one does not recognize all phenomena (*dharma*), there is nothing to be destroyed, and the accomplishment of *prajñā* is meager.

If the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) extensively destroys [delusions], it is like adding fuel to a fire. Furthermore, the explanation of the sequence is for the purpose of clarifying the aids to the path (*bodhipakṣa*).

For example, having attained the first dhyāna, one is already free from the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); continuing thus up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one is free from coarse afflictions and attains the severance of *prajñā*, thereby severing the ten subtle afflictions.

It is easy to eliminate afflictions [once they have been suppressed]. For example, an Arhat first eliminates the delusions of the three realms and subsequently attains *prajñā* to sever the residual habits (*vāsanā*) and enter the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, because directly employing *prajñā* to sever delusions is like drying out moisture, it is easy to obtain the auxiliary factors that serve as provisions for the path.

Moreover, the teaching of the gradual sequence is for the sake of training in the fearlessnesses; if one studies *prajñā* directly, it constitutes personal cultivation, yet it lacks the capacity to transform others. Therefore, one must study the sequence.
Furthermore, by answering questions as they arise, sentient beings gain faith and submission; subsequently, he reveals the true path.

Again, the reason for explaining the sequence is that when a Bodhisattva wishes to deliver sentient beings, the capacities and afflictions of those beings are infinite; therefore, one must study all dharmas exhaustively to recognize their ailments and identify the appropriate medicine.

Furthermore, the reason for explaining the sequence is to ensure consistency across various sutras and treatises; if there were inconsistencies regarding phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the underlying principle would likewise be compromised.

This results in obstruction. Furthermore, the reason for clarifying the sequential gate is to elucidate the Middle Way. If one were to clarify emptiness directly, it would not be the correct contemplation of the Middle Way.
As for the Middle Way: when the wise perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness, they do not even abide in emptiness, much less in non-emptiness.
By not abiding in either extreme and simultaneously illuminating both extremes, one then enters the true Path. Moreover, it is said in sequence:
The second point is a counter-question: Should one speak by departing from the sequence—that is, non-sequentially—or should one speak according to the sequence itself?
If one were to speak non-sequentially by departing from the sequence, then one should likewise be able to speak of emptiness separately from form.
If form is itself emptiness and emptiness does not depart from form, then it is precisely the sequence that is non-sequence; it is not a matter of departing from the sequence.
There is, indeed, that which is non-successive; yet one cannot speak of non-successiveness because it is unattainable. Thus the Sūtra says:

"Having cultivated the impermanence of form, it is unattainable," and so on, up to consciousness, which is likewise. Since the cultivation of succession is unattainable, this is precisely what is meant by non-successiveness.
To explain the meaning of the ten sections: the first five concern the mind’s aspiration and desire to seek a concentrated state of mind;
they are not yet the methods of actual practice. The latter five involve arising from self-understanding to initiate practice; these internal and external skillful means constitute true progress.

Without understanding, one cannot establish practice; understanding is the foundation of practice. Thus, the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-pūrvayoga-sūtra* says: "Great wisdom is the fundamental practice. Furthermore...

It is said: Without wisdom there is no dhyāna. Wisdom is itself understanding; dhyāna is itself practice. If one performs acts such as giving with a distracted mind amidst worldly affairs, their efficacy is slight.

However, if one restrains the mind through the stillness of dhyāna, one can give rise to the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) and rain down precious treasures throughout the great trichiliocosm, pervading the worlds of the ten directions to bestow them upon sentient beings. One should know that the cultivation of dhyāna is the practice of the Great Way.
Furthermore, the sequence for generating the ten intentions is as stated in the text (etc.). Fifth, regarding the "attaining of the mental factors" (*cittadharma*):
if one follows the doctrinal meaning, these are termed "object and wisdom" (*ālambana-jñāna*); however, here in the *Chanmen zhu*, they are termed "mental factors.

Sixth, regarding the "single layer of skillful means" (*upāya*): "skillful means" refers to being adept and resourceful; through internal and external skillful means, one prepares to advance toward attaining the proper state, skillfully employing the four [dhyānas].

One must first harmonize the mind through the *siddhānta* (established tenets), and only thereafter can one give rise to the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). This will be explained in detail below.

The tenfold elucidation of the meaning concludes with the sixth section; the seventh clarifies cultivation and realization. "Cultivation" refers to habitual practice, while "realization" refers to attainment.
This major section opens up many points, including the specific methods of cultivation and realization, beginning with the discussion of the stage of *Abhi*.

From the hells up to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and further from the four foundations of mindfulness through the practices of the Arhat—such as the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*) and the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*)—and again from the preliminary stages of hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*) leading to the nature of dhyāna according to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, as well as the cultivation and realization of the various stages (*bhūmi*), there are manifold differences.

The characteristics of cultivation are each distinct; the characteristics of realization are each distinct. Each and every one is subtle and precise, such that cause and effect are clearly distinguished.
The beginning and end are clearly visible; as the meaning is extensive, it will not be discussed further here. Question: Avīci is a realm of evil rebirths;

how can one distinguish the cultivation [of meditation] therein? Answer: It is generally termed "cultivation," yet there are many varieties, both genuine and false. A practitioner may cultivate dhyāna for the purpose of destroying the Triple Gem.
This is the cultivation of the *anabhi* dhyāna. Question: Dhyāna is the abandonment of evil. Since this person possesses an evil mind, how can they suddenly attain dhyāna?

The traditional interpretation states: "This person has heavy hindrances yet possesses sharp faculties; although their mind is evil at the moment of generating the resolve, if they collect the mind and enter dhyāna, they are able to give rise to it because their faculties are sharp.
The present interpretation is not thus. There are many kinds of dhyāna; it follows the ninety-six types of paths.
To be associated with these leads to the attainment of the demonic concentration of false dhyāna. This case is a manifestation of wrong view.

To attain and practice in accordance with them (and so forth) is like Devadatta’s cultivation of dhyāna, which is the dhyāna of Avīci hell. Whether one passes through the fundamental [dhyānas], the special excellences (*viśeṣa*), the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the practices of conduct (*caryā-caryā*), or the practices of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*), the characteristics of their cultivation differ in each instance; likewise, the false and the correct are distinct, even up to [the stage of] Bodhi.

In the various stages (*bhūmi*) of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the characteristics of cultivation and realization each have their own specific marks; a commentary on these shall consist of ten fascicles (and so forth).

Regarding the eighth [point], the manifestation of the retribution (*vipāka*): how does this retribution differ from cultivation and realization? Cultivation refers to the process of practice and is termed the "cause";

realization refers to the actual attainment and is termed the "fruit. This fruit is the fruit of habituation (*abhyāsa-phala*); at the time when the retribution is obtained, it is called the "fruit of retribution" (*vipāka-phala*).
From the Avīci Hell up to the stage of Buddhahood, one must demonstrate the retributive fruits (*vipāka-phala*) for each and every level.

If this refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*), it is clarified that they possess only the fruits of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*) and lack retributive fruits, because they have extinguished their physical bodies and eliminated their wisdom, leaving no place for rebirth.

If this refers to what is clarified in the Mahāyāna, such a person receives the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*) and likewise possesses retributive fruits. If this clarifies the Bodhisattva, [the following three...]

The ten noble dwellings of the wise are the retribution of fruition (*vipāka*). How could it be that their fruition cannot be distinguished? Even the Buddha may speak of "retribution. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"I pray to obtain the unsurpassed retribution. It also says: "By the cessation of this form, one obtains the eternal form.

This is also clearly a case of retribution. There are several scrolls that distinguish these matters. The ninth [section] concerns the arising of the teaching from dhyāna; herein, there is also the attainment of fruit through the practice of causes.

Having perfected one's own practice, one must further transform others. In the past, dwelling for a long time within birth and death, he studied all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)—whether sequentially or non-sequentially—and mastered them all.
Knowing the ailment and identifying the medicine, he established teachings according to what was appropriate.

If he established teachings for humans and devas, they mostly arose from the *sāmānyābhijñā-dhyāna* (the meditation of general supernormal knowledge). Why is this? Because this meditation involves profound contemplation of the five viscera (*pañca-kauṣṭhaya*). That is to say:
One is able to thoroughly comprehend the Five Elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). Above, they correspond to the five stars; below, they correspond to the five sacred peaks (*pañca-giri*).

Whether it be yin and yang, the eight trigrams (*aṣṭa-kheta*), the five constants (*pañca-dharma*), astronomy, geography, medical prescriptions, mathematics, military strategy, technical arts, calendrical calculations, ritual, or music—all these rely upon the five elements and the eight trigrams.
All such matters are fully understood through the Samādhi of Universal Clarity (*sarva-prakāśa-dhyāna*). Thus, one knows that [this samādhi] gives rise to the realms of humans and devas.
One emerges from this dhyāna by means of it. If, when practicing dhyāna, one’s *śīla* (ethical discipline) is not pure, *samādhi* will not manifest;

it is only by upholding the precepts that one attains the various dhyānas. At the moment dhyāna arises, one also gives rise to the *dhyāna-saṃvara-śīla* (precept associated with meditative concentration), and based on this, the *śīla-skandha* (aggregate of ethical discipline) is established.
Furthermore, the four dhyānas are themselves *samādhi*, and based on these, the *samādhi-skandha* (aggregate of concentration) is established. When practicing dhyāna, one contemplates the four...

Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): one must cultivate the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena and of persons—and only when the wisdom of contemplation is perfected can one perceive the principle and give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) state.

Therefore, the treasury of wisdom is established based upon these. There are two types of contemplation on emptiness: first, analytical emptiness (*bhedana-śūnyatā*); second, essential emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Based on analytical emptiness, the treasury of wisdom of the Tripitaka Teaching is established; based on essential emptiness, the treasury of wisdom of the Shared Teaching is established. Regarding the various [contemplations] within dhyāna...

Although phenomena are empty, a single mind encompasses the myriad practices; through provisional names and conceptual distinctions, one gives rise to names and characteristics—this is the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
If, within meditative concentration, one can contemplate the Middle Way, the truth of the emptiness of nature, then based on this, the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*) arises.
Furthermore, the Dharma-nature is itself Buddha-nature; based on this, the teaching of *Nirvāṇa* arises. (From the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*)

This is called the cave of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One contemplates the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) through meditation; this dharma-nature can deliver one from the two kinds of birth-and-death.

If one contemplates the principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is the "naturally pure self" (*prakṛti-viśuddha-ātman*); if one contemplates the perfect clarity of wisdom, it is the "perfectly pure self" (*pariśuddha-ātman*).
If one contemplates skillful means (*upāya*), then skillful means itself is the provisional skillfulness; it is the vehicle of skillful means. Based upon this, the teaching is established:

namely, the unsurpassed Mahāyāna of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* which unifies the three vehicles into one. Furthermore, because one contemplates the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) when practicing dhyāna, this is the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*).

Because one contemplates the path of provisional names (*prajñapti*), this is the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*). Because one contemplates the non-duality of emptiness and the provisional, [this is the knowledge of all aspects].
This refers to the Middle Way and the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); it is with reference to this that the teaching is established, and it is precisely Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, regarding the methods of contemplation within Dhyāna, one may practice according to a sequential order or at times according to a non-sequential order.

When transforming others, one responds to conditions through these means without fixed direction or restriction; this is the category of the Vaipulya sūtras such as the *Vimalakīrti*. Why is this? Because Vimalakīrti’s censure...
The refutation of worldly paths is not limited to a single method of transformation, as it does not consist of only one kind.

Furthermore, within the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings, there are instances where the Great and Small vehicles are presented side-by-side and contrasted with one another; this is precisely the intended meaning here.

Thus, we know that all teachings arise based upon dhyāna. Therefore, it is said that the turning of the Dharma-wheel by all Buddhas and their entry into nirvāṇa all occur within the four dhyānas. Based on...
Chan gives rise to the teachings; what teaching is not subsumed within it? Such points concerning the universal manifestation of the characteristics of all teachings can be understood by oneself.
There are generally two fascicles that clarify this meaning (and so forth). Tenth, regarding the conclusion and unification of the ultimate aim:

the preceding nine sections clarify Chan, from the ordinary person to the sage, with many successive discussions. To summarize their essential purport, it is simply the One Mind; therefore, [the text] explains it as follows.
The Treatise says: "Among all phenomena (*dharmas*), there are only name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*). If one wishes to contemplate them as they truly are, one should contemplate only name and form.

Form arises from the mind; to contemplate the nature of the mind alone is called the supreme concentration (*samādhi*). Thus we know that by investigating the mind, the mind encompasses all phenomena.
It is like obtaining a pearl or jade: all treasures are thereby acquired. It is like pulling a corner of a garment: every part moves."
Therefore, though the branches and currents are myriad, they all converge in the sea; likewise, while the characteristics of dhyāna are manifold, earnest discourse concerns only the mind.
By contemplating this nature of the mind, one realizes the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Thus, the ultimate source and essential summary reside solely herein. Such are the ten categories.
The first five sections of the analysis are esteemed by the School of Multiple Conditions (*saṃghāta*), as they clarify similarities and differences.

The sixth and seventh sections are the urgent essentials for the School of Subduing the Mind; these pertain to one's own practice and should not be explained to those who have not yet received instruction.

This is like the precepts and the mind of meditative concentration, which must not be bestowed recklessly. The subsequent stages of cultivation and realization are not attainable by beginners; there is no harm in explaining them [to those who are ready].
As in the Vinaya tradition, it is permitted to receive the five minor precepts (and so forth).

This concludes the explanation of the first major section. Regarding the clarification of the general meaning through the exclusion of what is not [the path], there are ten types in total, as fully explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (*Zhiguan*).
I shall now briefly clarify one or two examples: for instance, practicing dhyāna for the sake of seeking peace and happiness belongs to the six [perfections].

The mind of the desire-realm heavens consists of forming intentions to guard and maintain [the precepts], abandoning evil and cultivating good, and aspiring for peace and happiness; this is termed the mind belonging to the human realm.
Therefore, the experience of retribution is only obtained through the convergence of conditions. If it were accomplished by a spontaneous mind, there would be no need for protection. Why is this?
Because one attains the flavor of *dhyāna*, one experiences spontaneous joy. One may enter *dhyāna* for three or five days without arising from it;
even when one does arise and emerge from contemplation, there is spontaneous bliss. If one generates the resolve to seek this, it is called the "Heavenly Mind" (*deva-citta*).

Subsequently, the retribution of heaven arrives naturally and spontaneously, without the need for strenuous effort; therefore, this mind is named the Heavenly Mind. To take an analogy, it is like a dried cowhide. Although...

Forcefully rolling up and unfolding [the mind] without following its natural disposition is like *manasikāra* (mental attention); it is like the hide of a cow’s brain, which is soft and pliable when pulled or touched.

This is like entering *dhyāna* (meditative absorption); even after emerging from concentration, there remains a lingering flavor. The precepts and generosity thus cultivated differ from those performed with a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), and so forth.
Furthermore, to directly seek power is the mind of Māra; it is like Māra being attached to karmic retribution. Upon seeing a person leave the realm [of the senses], he immediately...

This comes to obstruct and destroy [the path]. Just as people of the present age possess great power and receive the fruits of their retribution, if someone opposes them, they are able to harm others.
Furthermore, delighting in various views is the mind of an outsider (*tīrthika*).

Desiring to give rise to wisdom through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to disparage others and exalt oneself—as described in the *Liṅqimí* (Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta) causal narrative—is why meditative stillness can give rise to what is false.

Regarding right and wrong wisdom: when one originally grasps principles through erroneous means, if one now polishes them with a tranquil mind, that erroneous wisdom will immediately arise and become wrong view.
When the mind was originally correct, if one uses meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to harmonize it, right wisdom will immediately arise; such right wisdom requires no further discernment.

Meditating with a deviant mind is why it must be distinguished [from true meditation]. Furthermore, if a person in the secular world possesses the three minds of seeking pleasure, delighting in power, and delighting in views, one judges their cause by evaluating the relative strength of these states. If, despite seeking pleasure, the force of that pleasure is dominant, it belongs to the mind of Māra.
If there is merely a delight in pleasure accompanied by a slight degree of purity, it belongs to the mind of Brahmā. If there is a delight in pleasure and also compassion for others...

When it is directed toward an object, it is the mind of Brahmā; if one delights in various views, it belongs to the non-Buddhists. These three aspects of the mind are combined, and the cause is determined according to whichever is predominant (and so forth).

Furthermore, directly regarding the minds of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they are themselves categorized into three types: first, those who practice perversely; second, those who involve worldly affairs while also engaging with others;

and third, those who possess both of the above. When these names are applied broadly to the time when false wisdom arises, they constitute three types of non-Buddhists: the first is the "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*).

Second is the attainment of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); third is the *Veda*, which subsumes the aforementioned two. Generally, these three types of celestial minds are also considered non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).

"Delighting in power" refers to supernatural powers; "delighting in various views" refers to omniscience (*sarvajña*); and "possessing a pure mind while also involving human [affairs]" refers to the *Veda*.
Whether in their general or specific aspects, their application of the mind is deviant and improper. Therefore, they are not among the vehicles (*yāna*). This is the reversal.

Returning from the heterodox to the orthodox: when confronting and refuting the three types of external paths at the time of awakening to the cause, these are precisely the three kinds of *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness).

Attaining the fruit constitutes the three kinds of *vimokṣa* (liberations). Refuting the heterodox to reveal the orthodox (*etc.*). However, while it is conventionally judged that the ten mental states constitute the cause, why must it necessarily be so?
For example, falling into hell involves many varieties and does not consist of only a single path; here, we cite the most prominent [cases] to illustrate.

This is merely the beginning of the exposition. Even for the Two Vehicles entering into principle, there are many types of Dharma-gates; I have briefly cited several practices to illustrate the terminology.
Because they practice these various [methods], they are inevitably included therein. If one were to sequentially exclude what is incorrect:

first, through "Cessation" (śamatha), one excludes the errors of the three miserable realms, yet does not exclude those of humans and devas. If one proceeds to clarify the Two Vehicles, it is simply that their nine mental states are excluded. If...

The Mahāyāna is precisely the non-duality of the two extremes; it is the "neither" of all ten [categories]. If one were to apply the negation of non-sequential distinctions, one would further differentiate within the bodhisattva’s mind;
this is fully detailed in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Now, as we rely on the sequential order, these ten practices constitute the negation of non-distinctions.
Question: Does the arousal of this mind immediately constitute the karma? Or must one realize dhyāna and fulfill one's aspirations before it is established?
[Question: Is it karma? [Answer: In the Hīnayāna, the movement of the seven limbs constitutes karma; the initial arousal of the thought is not yet karma.

In the Mahāyāna, it is clarified that if one gives rise to even a single thought of evil, the calamity will lead to the Avīci hell; regardless of whether the deed is subsequently carried out or not, the arousal of the thought itself is karma.

[Question: Should this not have degrees of lightness and heaviness? [Answer: If it remains at the stage of the initial arousal of the thought, it is indeterminate karma; if the deed is accomplished, it is determinate karma. [Question: If...
The practice of dhyāna requires the destruction of the desire realm. One may give rise to the first dhyāna; only when meditative concentration is perfected does one take birth in the higher realms.

If one gives rise to an evil thought intending to destroy the Triple Gem, why would one fall into hell before that act is completed? Answer: When performing evil, it is like a collapsing mountain; thus, the moment an evil thought arises, the karma is already established.

When performing good, it is like a construction project; one must initiate the dhyāna before being born [in the higher realms]. Furthermore, the hells belong to the same realm (dhātu); once the thought is initiated...

The mind immediately falls [into error]. The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is a distinct realm; one must first develop meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) before being born there. Now, we distinguish ten kinds of false minds, which differ in whether they constitute karma or do not constitute karma.
This mind is precisely what is called "non-[virtuous]. If one does not recognize it, the continuity will remain unbroken, whereby karmic bonds are formed and one is led into rebirth.
Therefore, it must be abandoned. Question: Are these ten non-[virtuous] states identical to or different from the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)? Answer:

The ten realms open up both the ordinary and the sacred; the ten minds open up the ordinary while merging with the sacred. This is to clarify that the two extremes of bondage and liberation are both non-existent.
Second, to manifest what is correct is called the "Correct Elucidation of the Great Meaning of Cultivating Dhyāna," which is precisely the arousal of the bodhicitta.

The mind has four types: first, generating the mind by taking as its object phenomena that arise and perish through the conditions of causes and conditions; second, generating the mind by taking as its object the principle of true emptiness;
third, generating the mind by taking as its object conventional truth and provisional names; and fourth, generating the mind by taking as its object the middle way and the dharma-realm.
If the aforementioned various errors are present, they mostly involve taking as objects non-causes, false causes, one’s own wholesome causes, or the cause of seeking only one's own liberation.
Regarding causes and conditions: they are not the true causes and conditions. Because they lack great compassion, they cannot act for the sake of sentient beings; thus, they are not the bodhicitta.
When a Bodhisattva perceives that sentient beings give rise to ten kinds of false and unequal causes and conditions, he gives rise to great compassion on their account.
This is because sentient beings fail to recognize the true causes and conditions, and consequently give rise to nine kinds of evil. Evil is precisely the accumulation (*samudaya*). Accumulation...
This invites the fruit of suffering. Because Bodhisattvas wish to uproot the suffering and its origins for these sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion and establish two vows:
"I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings"—this arises from uprooting suffering; "I vow to sever immeasurable afflictions"—this is produced from uprooting the origin of suffering.
Furthermore, because sentient beings possess suffering and its origin, there is no Path or Cessation, which are the causes for transcending the world.

Fruit. Because one desires to bring about the cessation of suffering through the Path, one gives rise to great compassion and establishes two vows: "I vow to know the infinite dharma-gates" corresponds to the Path;
"I vow to achieve supreme Buddha-enlightenment" corresponds to Cessation. These are the conditions and the primary causes for giving rise to vows and generating the bodhicitta.
Once the mind has been correctly generated, one's practice and vows will not be partial; this is called [the correct path].

This is because one arouses the mind to practice dhyāna by relying on the causal conditions of the True Cause. Next, regarding those who arouse the mind by relying on the principle of True, Pure Emptiness:
this simply means relying on the previous contemplation of the True Cause to realize that all things are empty. Sentient beings, however, are deluded and claim they are not empty;

because they do not know emptiness, they give rise to ten kinds of deviant existence. Existence is precisely *saṃudaya* (the origin of suffering); because of *saṃudaya*, suffering is summoned. For this reason...
From this, one gives rise to great compassion and establishes two vows. This accumulation of suffering is, in its very essence, emptiness.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Form itself is emptiness; emptiness itself is form. Form and emptiness, emptiness and form—these are non-dual and without distinction.

This is called the Middle Way. The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states: "One who can explain dependent origination skillfully extinguishes all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). There are two kinds of extinction.

There are two kinds of cessation: first, the cessation of the wholesome; second, the cessation of the unwholesome. The cessation of the unwholesome refers to the analytical contemplation of emptiness (*vibhāga-dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*);

it is empty because form is extinguished. The cessation of the wholesome refers to the realization that form itself is emptiness; it is not that emptiness arises from the extinction of form. This is what is meant by the cessation of the wholesome.
Desiring to bring sentient beings to such a path of cessation, one gives rise to great compassion and establishes two vows. Having thus recognized the primary causes and conditions, [one proceeds].

Because it is emptiness itself, the arousal of the mind, the practices, and the vows all take the Truth (paramārtha-satya) as their object. This is the pure arousal of the bodhicitta by taking the Truth as its object.

Next, regarding the arousal of the mind by taking conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as its object: although there are immeasurable marks of provisional names and distinctions, sentient beings do not recognize them and falsely give rise to discrimination, producing the perverse and the evil.
The followers of the Two Vehicles merely empty the mind, yet that which they have not reached they take to be emptiness.
Realization. It is here that the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and formulates vows (and so forth).

Furthermore, the bodhicitta generated by taking the Middle Way as its object is also known by various synonymous names, such as the mind of the true principle of the Middle Way, ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), *amala-vijñāna*, buddha-nature, suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the true mark (*dharmatā*), non-abiding, and non-arising. As [it is said in] the *Devatā*...

Śakra has many names, yet all are free from bondage and liberated from the various dual extremes—mundane and supramundane, with-outflow and without-outflow, conditioned and unconditioned, and so forth.
Therefore, he is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, neither conditioned nor unconditioned. To negate these two extremes is called the "Middle.
This is precisely emptiness, stillness, and cessation, having nothing upon which to rely or lean. It is the Middle that clarifies itself by depending on the extremes.
It is unattainable; its severance is called the Middle. One who can act thus universally grasps the principle of the unsurpassed, true, and perfect reality, which is designated as the Way (*mārga*).
This principle is neither cause nor effect, neither beginning nor end, neither arising nor non-arising, and neither the Way nor non-Way.
Pure as empty space, it accords with things and adapts to conditions, yet it speaks of cause, effect, the Way, the mind, and so forth.
Why is this so? Because the nature of the minds of sentient beings is luminous wisdom like the sun, it is said that they are covered by darkness as black as lacquer.
When one first resolves to attain enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), one eliminates the deviations of the two extremes; manifesting the principle of the Middle Way is called the "cause" (*hetu*).

To bring this principle to ultimate completion is called the "fruit" (*phala*). To penetrate this principle is called the "path" (*mārga*). Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* states:
The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true nature of all phenomena.
However, this mind of correct contemplation—which cannot be destroyed, is immovable, and does not regress—is called the "true nature. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"That which is immovable and non-regressive is the mind, and it is named *sattva*. If one enters the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) without attaining this mind, none of them are called *bodhi*."
If one enters the successive stages of dhyāna with this mind, all are called *pāramitās*. Entering the dharmas of the two vehicles and ordinary beings is all called Mahāyāna.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "In the mind of successive stages, one speaks of sentient beings;
how then should one cultivate and practice *prajñā*? The Buddha said: "Because the various mental activities of the mind do not function, it is called practicing *prajñā*."
This is called "arising" and "cultivation. It is precisely the practice of non-arising, non-exertion, and non-cultivation.

When this mind arises, it spontaneously co-arises with objectless compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*). For the sake of sentient beings, one preaches this Dharma of reliance, causing them to escape the suffering of bondage to the two extremes;
this is termed "objectless great compassion. It is [the realization of] the unshakable true reality (*dharmatā*) of sentient beings.
Joy is called great loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings falsely reckon existence within non-existence and reckon a self within non-self;
there are thirty-two such types. For their sake, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion (*karuṇā*). Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Within all dharmas, there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss. One should know that the principle of the true mark (*tathatā*) spontaneously accords with loving-kindness and compassion."
It arises. Not only does it possess this compassion, but it possesses all [virtues] as well; therefore, it is said: "Although all phenomena are empty, the single mind possesses the myriad practices.
When sentient beings attain happiness, it is not that the Tathāgata bestows happiness upon them;

they possess it themselves. It is like a poor woman’s gold being uncovered by her weeding and digging. The principle of uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness is likewise so. Furthermore, from itself...

Attaining bliss is self-arising; the Tathāgata bestowing it is other-arising. [This is refuted] by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and so forth. Since these four natures do not exist, one speaks of "self-bliss," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the three preceding types of generating the bodhicitta, although they now refer to the three kinds of Four Noble Truths, the three *pāramitās*, the three causes and three fruits, and the three kinds of vows, they are not termed "extensive. Now, as for the Middle Way...
The mind takes the unconditioned Four Noble Truths as its object; encompassing the Four Great Vows, it gives rise to the vow of resolution.

Thus, it is called a "Great Vow. Question: Why is it not [merely] a "vow" if it does not accord with principle? Is it the case that all [compassion] arises from taking sentient beings and dharmas as objects to give rise to compassion?
Answer: It is like a woman who is deceitful and crooked; therefore, it is not called a "Great Vow. If, however, it is the Middle Way...
This compassion accords with principle and is not called flattery. As stated in the *Mahāprajāpatī-sūtra*, even women may possess such non-flattery.

This is the compassion of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); compassion is itself the Tathāgata. It is like a magnet attracting iron: apart from the stone there is no attraction, and apart from the attraction there is no stone;
the attraction itself is the stone. Just so, compassion itself is the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called the "Great Vow" (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). Furthermore, it is like...

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If one calculates that all phenomena possess a fixed nature—where 'nature' means a fixed reality, existing substantially and unchangeable—then there would be no four purities, the four practices, the noble paths and fruits, nor the Three Jewels, the causes and effects of the supramundane, nor any worldly dharmas such as sin and merit.
If one calculates that all phenomena are a fixed emptiness, one falls into nihilism; likewise, [there would be nothing]."
Regarding the dharmas of the causes and effects of the mundane and supramundane noble ones, they are merely empty, false, and inverted, leading to cyclic existence and self-inflicted injury.

If one can cultivate the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, realize the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and deeply understand suffering and its origin, then the contemplation that can treat these is itself the Path and Cessation.
Thus, the Three Jewels, the Four Truths, and the Eightfold Path are all quiescent and remain entirely free from destruction. Therefore—

It is said that one does not destroy conventional designations while explaining the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; this is called generating the bodhicitta through the Middle Way of conditions.
Regarding the vow to know the inexhaustible gateways for discerning the Dharma: a "gate" is so named because it enables passage, and this passage is itself the Path (*mārga*). It is unsurpassed.
The Buddha-way and the vow for its fulfillment—how do these differ? Answer: The Dharma-gate is explained horizontally; the Buddha-way is discussed vertically. Question:
Nirvāṇa is also called the Way, and the true reality (bhūtatathatā) is also called the Way, because the Buddha has come from the Great Way of true reality.

Prajñā is also called the Way. What is the relationship between these three? Answer: If one discusses them in terms of the three virtues (triguṇa), neither the Dharmakāya nor the Prajñā is [the ultimate].
Liberation is also not [separate]; neither identity nor difference applies to them. When these three dharmas are fully present, it is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*);
how could one discuss them in isolation? Now, if we discuss the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) as its own essence: from the Dharma-body, practice arises; this practice is precisely Prajñā.
Prajñā is named the Path (*mārga*), which leads through to Nirvāṇa. Here, we take the ultimate destination reached by this vertical progression and name it Nirvāṇa; it is unsurpassed.
The Way. The place where one attains deliverance is precisely Prajñā; it is called a Dharma-gate (and so forth). Question:
The Middle Way and True Reality (*bhūtatathatā*) are not created by Buddhas, devas, humans, or asuras. Why, then, do you speak of "arising"? Answer:

Although they are not produced by any [agent], that which was hidden is called the "Treasury" (*garbha*), and its manifestation is called "the body that can act. As explained above regarding realization, when one waits for what was hidden to no longer remain unarisen, this is termed "arising. Question: Is it...?
Question: Since the mind can be generated through meditation (*dhyāna*), yet one speaks only of generating the mind through aspiration toward the treatises, what is the answer?

Answer: Both meanings apply. If one is able to aspire, it is called "understanding" (*adhimukti*). Understanding is the root of practice. Because [the mind] advances through meditation, all such instances are termed "generating.

Question: The bodhicitta is neither eternal (*śāśvata*) nor annihilated (*uccheda*). Does there exist a separate principle apart from this, or does it exhaust these notions of eternity and annihilation while being said to be "neither eternal"?
That which is neither annihilation nor permanence is called the Middle Way. Answer: This refers to the two gates of emptiness and existence (and so forth).
Question: Why is not the "True" taken as the Buddha-nature? Answer: The Middle Way is the ultimate; the True and the Conventional are merely the objective realms of the Buddha-nature.

Furthermore, speaking from the perspective of principle (*li*), all phenomena possess the nature of bliss; why then single out only the True and the Middle? Answer: This is according to the teachings (*jiao*).
"One who sees the truth" has not yet seen the Buddha-nature. Question: "If all possess the nature of peace and bliss, do grasses and trees have it as well? Answer:

"For one who enters into principle and awakens to the equal Dharma-realm, there is no further distinction between person and grass; for one who has not yet awakened, these are said to be distinct matters."

It is like the various things in a dream; once one has awakened, they are no longer there. Question: Delusion regarding the true reality (dharmatā) gives rise to suffering and its origin; understanding the true reality gives rise to the path and its cessation.

Since the path and cessation are different from suffering and its origin, and suffering and its origin are not the path and cessation, is it not also the case that suffering and its accumulation are not the true reality, and the path and cessation likewise are not?

Answer: It is precisely delusion regarding the true reality that constitutes suffering and its accumulation; it is precisely understanding the true reality that constitutes the path and its cessation. This is analogous to the freezing of water due to cold.
Water becomes ice; when it is warmed and melted, ice becomes water again. The cessation of the path (*mārganirodha*) is also like this.

There is no separate middle way distinct from the cessation of the path, nor is there anything different from suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*). This is because there is no dharma outside of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); therefore, they are not separate. Question:
Cold causes water to congeal into ice; ice is a metaphor for the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*), and cold is a metaphor for adversity.

Now, melting the ice back into water—water is a metaphor for the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*), while warmth is a metaphor for the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). How could there be a Middle Way apart from the path and cessation? Answer: Not so.
Cold is the accumulation, ice is suffering, warmth is the path, and melting is cessation. How could there be water existing separately from warmth and melting?

Since the analogy of water is thus established, one need not further seek a middle way. Question: Is there a difference between the bodhicitta and the vow (praṇidhāna)? Answer: The mind is the essential substance (svabhāva).
That which arises from this substance as its function (vṛtti) is called the vow. Question: The treatise states that "bodhicitta is called the Great Vow.
Now, the Four Great Vows are also called vows. In this case, then, substance and function are not distinct. Answer: This function arises from the substance; it is not...

They are distinct in their characteristics, yet they are collectively termed "vows" because both the essence-vow and the practice-vow share this designation. Question: If vows can manifest the essence, then the six perfections also manifest the essence;

are these what is meant here by "vows"? Answer: That which manifests the essence through vows refers to the Four Great Vows; that which manifests the essence through practice refers to the Six Perfections.
While their meaning in manifesting [the essence] is the same, their function as practice and vow constitutes their difference.
The second section, which correctly clarifies the purpose of practicing dhyāna, is as follows: the previous bodhicitta is the eyes, while the current practice is the feet.
Because both eyes and feet are cultivated, one is able to enter the cool pond. From this point onward, there are three parts:
first, from "In order to fulfill the four vows" onwards is the practice of conduct; second, from "In what dharma-gate do I now abide? onwards is relying on dhyāna as the gate; third...
The question, "Why not practice all ten perfections? asks why this [text] clarifies that dhyāna subsumes all dharmas.
Now, at the beginning of practice, one generates four vows. Four analogies are used to illustrate these four vows, as in the text.

Next, to clarify relying on dhyāna as the gateway: this is likewise for fulfilling the four vows. Just as one must enter dhyāna in order to fulfill these vows, the section from the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvid*) onwards clarifies the fulfillment of the first vow. The six supernormal powers arise from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), which constitutes the adornment of merit;
the four analytical knowledges constitute the adornment of wisdom. Previously, one has already used supernormal powers to subdue arrogance.
In order to preach the Dharma so that beings may awaken to the Way, the Great Sūtra says: "First move them by means of concentration; afterwards, extract them by means of wisdom.

Furthermore, there are three ways in which supernormal powers (abhijñā) are developed. In the Shared Teaching (pāṭha-sāmānya), supernormal powers are developed from meditative states such as the liberations (vimokṣa), the bases of mastery (abhibhv-āyatana), the knowledge resulting from vows (praṇidhi-jñāna), and the summit of existence (bhavāgra).

In the Distinct Teaching (pṛthag-vyākaraṇa), supernormal powers are developed from meditative states such as the self-nature samādhis (svabhāva-samādhi). Both of these cases involve development from meditation. Question: What are the five and six [supernormal powers]?

[Question: Is there a difference? [Answer: This is spoken in reference to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). When the active afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed, it is called the "penetration of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*);

it may also be designated as "six. However, because the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted, it is called "five. In the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), once one has attained the severance of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is also called "six";
yet, as this is not yet ultimate, it is called "five. Thus, both "five" and "six" are applicable. From the point of wishing to sever the afflictions onward, this explains the second [section].

Aspiration: Now, the severing of delusions must necessarily rely on wisdom (*prajñā*), yet wisdom does not open up without meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). A great scripture states: "One who lacks concentration will fall headlong from level ground;

their hands write different characters, their mouth proclaims different words, and their body traverses different paths. Therefore, one knows that among the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), the category of concentration must also be mentioned.
Why then is it said [here] only "wisdom"? Furthermore, in the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the seven causes of the untainted (*anāsrava*) depend upon concentration.

[The practitioner] abandons [wrong] views. Based on the nine stages, they abandon the afflictions of the realm of desire. Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, one gives rise to a semblance of understanding based solely on *svabhāva-dhyāna* (meditation on intrinsic nature);
therefore, it is called the "hearing and reflection" (*śruta-cintā*) that precedes the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. By means of this, one enters all meditations. There are three kinds of all meditations.
Abiding in dhyāna in the present life means that one gives rise to the true vision of principle, abandoning attachment to flavor and all mental signs (*nimitta*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"In the first stage (*bhūmi*), even the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) and their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) are simultaneously exhausted without remainder. This refers to the complete exhaustion of the pervasive [afflictions] through the correct accumulation [of merit and wisdom].

Furthermore, it involves the partial severing of specific delusions and the partial arising of true gnosis (*jñāna*), as illustrated by the analogy of the eyes, and so forth. Thus, one sees the principle and brings it forth.
The first is called the dhyāna of happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). The second is the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the lineage of birth;
it is the concentration that increases the Middle Way and constitutes the adornment of merit. The third is the dhyāna for benefiting sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva abides in this dhyāna, they benefit others through its meaning, acting as their companions and causing them to be free from all sufferings. By merely giving rise to this single dhyāna—
It possesses three meanings. Up to the point of pure dhyāna, when a bodhisattva abides in this dhyāna, they attain the fruit of great bodhi;
all of these are contained within dhyāna. Therefore, we know that dhyāna can fulfill the second vow. From the phrase "desiring to know the dharma-gates" onwards is the explanation of the third vow.
Regarding the "dharma-gates one desires to know," there are two types: the practices of the right path and the auxiliary path, which are wisdom.

Although these are auxiliary paths to enlightenment, one should temporarily rely on dhyāna to give rise to the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*). The true path consists solely in the profound contemplation of phenomena and the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

While all auxiliary gates can give rise to wisdom, they likewise employ dhyāna. If the Sautrāntikas merely contemplate conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), that which is signless and true emptiness is called right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*).

Although these two differ, both must be attained through the cultivation of dhyāna; this applies even to the Lesser Vehicle, as when the Buddha sat beneath the Bodhi tree and contemplated the Four [Noble Truths].
Through the thirty-four moments of mind of the four truths, one severs the fetters and realizes the Path, turns the Wheel of Dharma, and enters Nirvana. The fire of the outflows consumes the body;

like a leather bag filled with sand, it benefits all beings. There is nothing that does not exist within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, this is spoken from the perspective of the Mahāyāna.

Dhyāna is the greatest, like a king. The mundane primary and auxiliary practices, the supramundane primary and auxiliary practices, and the supreme primary and auxiliary practices are all subsumed within dhyāna.
Thus, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Yingluo jing) states: "The Buddha, relying on pure dhyāna, attained the fruit of Great Bodhi.

Furthermore, he entered the King Samādhi to preach the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and likewise for the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, he entered the cave of profound meditative concentration.
All sentient beings possess the characteristic of total extinction; to cause them not to undergo further extinction is itself Great Nirvāṇa. When has this ever not been dhyāna?
At times it manifests as entering [meditative absorption], and at times it does not manifest as entering it, yet the mind is always in samādhi.

Because there is no time when one is not in samādhi while manifesting in the Buddha-lands of the two vehicles, we know that within dhyāna all Dharma-gates are fully contained. This is the teaching of the conventional truth according to the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*).

The gates are the phenomena (*dharma*), while the Dharma-gate of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the principle (*li*). In the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), both the ultimate and the conventional are phenomena, while the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is the principle.
Samādhis of such phenomena and principles are all subsumed within dhyāna; therefore, one knows that by practicing dhyāna, one can know all Dharma-gates.
This constitutes the fulfillment of the third vow. Regarding the fourth vow, which follows from "seeking to fulfill the Buddha-way," the Buddha-way is none other than *nirvāṇa*.
The analysis of its horizontal and vertical dimensions is as previously explained (*et cetera*). There are two kinds of *nirvāṇa*.

There are two types of attainment: partial and complete. When those of the Hīnayāna sever the afflictions of the desire realm and are reborn in the Brahma Heaven, this is also called "liberation" and carries the meaning of "partial extinction.

Therefore, it is said that in the Brahma Heaven, the afflictions of the desire realm no longer exist. If the bonds of the "son" (the defilements) are severed, it is called "Nirvāṇa with remainder," which is also termed "partial attainment.
If one abandons the bonds of the "fruit" (the physical body), it is called "Nirvāṇa without remainder"; this constitutes the complete attainment of the Hīnayāna. As it is said:
Is it not the case that this Dharma can only be fully perfected through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)?

If those of the Mahāyāna possess a portion [of this], and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) likewise possess a portion, both are termed "Nirvāṇa with remainder. Why is this? Because deep delusions have not yet been severed.
If one dwells in the dharma-pleasure of *svabhāva-dhyāna* and perceives only the Truth, this is called "Nirvāṇa with remainder. If one attains *samādhi*...
Bhadrika, being fully endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom, is said to have attained *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

From this state, he spontaneously enters the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience), which is called *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvana). Although it is non-abiding, it is not yet ultimate; it becomes ultimate only upon reaching the stage of complete purity.

Question: Regarding the five abodes, which are heavy and which are light? Answer: They are both heavy and both light. The four abodes deviate from principle and give rise to opposition; this is what is called "heavy."
This is what is meant by "heavy. Because ignorance is an obstruction to principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), its failure to give rise to resistance is called "light.

Furthermore, ignorance is the root that is severed by Buddha-wisdom, and is thus called "heavy. The four abidings (*catur-vāsana*) are branches and twigs that are repelled by expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), and are thus called "light.
The Master of the Treatise says: "Superior-superior wisdom severs inferior-inferior; inferior-inferior wisdom severs superior-superior. This takes the four abidings as heavy and ignorance as light.

Answer: It is merely because the name of the fruit is applied to the causal stage. Question: *Nirvāṇa* is the fruit; the followers of the Two Vehicles attain what is named *nirvāṇa*. For what reason is this not called a *pāramitā*? Answer: The term *nirvāṇa* means cessation. The followers of the Two Vehicles seek only to escape suffering; they see the cessation of the suffering of views and afflictions as being *nirvāṇa*. However, [true] *nirvāṇa* is the extinction of all outflows (*āsrava*) and the exhaustion of all conditioned phenomena. Because their attainment does not reach the ultimate limit, it is not designated as a *pāramitā*. Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva practices the six perfections throughout the three periods of time, the Two Vehicles do not practice them in such a manner. Therefore, although they attain a state of cessation, it is not called a *pāramitā*. Moreover, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the six perfections is for the sake of benefiting others, whereas the Two Vehicles’ practice is for their own benefit alone. For these reasons, it is not called a *pāramitā*. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s practice of the six perfections is for the sake of attaining the Great Nirvāṇa, whereas the Two Vehicles’ practice is for the sake of attaining the Lesser Nirvāṇa. Question: Since the three contemplations have already manifested from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, why does one become submerged in emptiness at the seventh stage?

Answer: When a Bodhisattva first attains full realization, the principle of emptiness revealed by the three contemplations is extremely profound. At times, they may become particularly proficient in this principle, or they may specifically employ it to transform others.
This is like reciting a scripture: initially, all three sections are recited together, but later one focuses exclusively on a single section. At the seventh stage, one investigates...

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) should also be understood by analogy with this. From the third section on detailed analysis (*viniścaya*) onwards, there are four questions and answers: first, to clarify that dhyāna is vast and all-encompassing;
second, to analyze it in relation to the four dharmas based on its reliance upon the fundamental [dhyānas]; third, to show that while "dhyāna" is a single name, it possesses further distinctions;

and fourth, furthermore, the first question concerns how dhyāna is great and contains all dharmas, while the second question concerns its relationship to wisdom (*jñāna*), concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth. Third...

Cultivation through reflection (*cintā-bhāvanā*) pervades all phenomena. "Reflection" is simply another name for *dhyāna* (meditative concentration); therefore, it is designated by the term "dhyāna. Regarding "wisdom, concentration," and so forth:

within the four *dhyānas*, there are eighteen factors (*aṅga*). Four are comprised within the factor of "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*), which is categorized as concentration; fourteen are comprised within wisdom.
Because the complete possession of both concentration and wisdom can give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*), the commentators say: "Wisdom is [the perception of] suffering..."
Difficult practice is certainly pleasant and easy practice; there is also pleasant difficult practice and painful easy practice.
If within wisdom one gives rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava), it is painful easy practice; if one does not give rise to it, it is painful difficult practice. It is the same regarding pleasure.

The Sāṃkhyas say that pain opposes penetration while pleasure does not oppose penetration. This is based on wisdom: pleasure opposes penetration, whereas pleasure does not oppose penetration. This is according to...

Regarding concentration (*samādhi*): only that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) does not arise within concentration; as is appropriate for wisdom (*prajñā*), since the four dhyānas possess both this concentration and wisdom, they are called "equal" (*sama*).
Other dharmas are not so; thus they are not called equal. Question: By what are the four dhyānas defined as having an "equal" objective sphere (*ālambana*)? Answer:

In the first dhyāna, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the objective spheres. This continues up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which has neither perception nor non-perception as its objective sphere.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is taken as the object. Question: If perception and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*) are taken as the objects, does one observe the object with this mind of perception and investigation, or does one observe the object with a single mind?

If one observes with a single mind, it cannot be called "a single mind" [if it possesses these factors]. If one observes the object with perception and investigation, how can there be an observation of that observation?
Answer: The Saṃkhyas clarify that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitta*) arise simultaneously; this is...

There is a mind capable of observation that observes the objects of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). Regarding the proponents of the *pudgala* (person), they clarify that there is a distinct, pure, and subtle mind that observes the objects of vitarka and vicāra (*etc.*).

As for the essence (*tattva*): according to the proponents of the *pudgala*, all five factors are skillful means (*upāya*), while the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*) constitutes the essence.
According to the "Counters" (*gaṇanā-vādins*), desire, mindfulness, and so forth are the skillful means, while all five factors constitute the essence. This is the usage in the *Śāstra*.

Regarding this treatise: according to the *Abhidharmakośa* school (the Cheng-lun masters), because the four factors [of the first dhyāna] are coarse when considered as the means (*upāya*) prior to the actual state of concentration (*samādhi*), they do not constitute its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
According to the Sautrāntikas (the Shu-jen), the five factors are the means external to the state of concentration; since they arise from these, they all constitute the essential nature.

Now, in explaining this, there are both a general nature and specific natures. That which is common to all is the general nature: a single mind. Applying the general to the specific, the first dhyāna has vitarka and vicāra as its essential nature. The second...

The first dhyāna takes internal purity as its essence; the second dhyāna takes joy (*sukha*) as its essence; the third dhyāna takes bliss (*sukha*) as its essence; and the fourth dhyāna takes immovability (*āniñjya*) as its essence.

By defining these distinct essences, they distinguish them from the single mind (*ekacitta*). This [first dhyāna] is the single mind characterized by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); this [fourth dhyāna] is the single mind within the state of immovability.

The masters of the *Abhidharma-śāstra* clarify their commonality, while the masters of the *Saṃkhyā* school combine them with wisdom (*prajñā*). As it says in the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Yingluo jing*): "The five factors are all skillful means; the sixth..."

The *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) takes the five factors as its substance; since these are all coarse and belong equally to the stage of preparation (*prayoga*), it takes their stillness and subtlety as its substance.

This, however, is merely a general explanation. As for the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), which lack a forest of factors, how is this so? First, they generally take the concentrated mind as their substance.
Second, if one brings the object into consideration to define a distinct substance, it is like taking the clarity of the "infinite space" (*ākāśānantya-āyatana*) as one.

The mind takes the realm of emptiness as its essence. The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Yingluo) states: "The four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) have five factors, namely: perception (*saṃjñā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).
This applies universally to all [the dhyānas]. Thus, it remains a general principle; there are no distinct individual factors such as those characterized in the four dhyānas.

Furthermore, regarding the intermediate dhyāna and the stage of access (*anāgamya*): if categorized according to the four dhyānas, they should all pertain to the four intermediate stages and the four stages of access.
[The *Śāriputrābhidharma*] sets this forth in detail (etc.). However, because the intermediate [dhyāna] and the *anāgamya* are similar in their characteristics, they are both grouped together as one.
The *anāgamya* is the "one middle" (*eka-madhya*). It is called "middle" because it is the central pillar between the preceding dhyānas.
The Master of Nanyue referred to this as the "detached meditative ground" (*vairāgya-bhūmi*), for it is detached from the first and second [dhyānas]; hence it is called "detached meditation."
This stage is also called *mīṣakṣepa-dhyāna* (the dhyāna of casting away). It consists merely of a single state of stillness. This joy is a point of regression in dhyāna;

it is like a man who has sent away his wife before obtaining a new one—he loses his pleasure and gives rise to sorrow. This regression may result in returning to the first dhyāna, or it may cause one to lose the first dhyāna altogether.

If one can forcefully apply contemplative practice and develop deep revulsion for the lower level, one will enter the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and give rise to the second dhyāna. Within this [state], however—
There are those with wisdom who observe but have little concentration, nor are they equal in both. Next, the cultivation through reflection (*bhāvanā*) is explained.

This term applies universally to all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), which are collectively termed "cultivation through reflection. Furthermore, if one were to apply specific names to specific categories, the general term "cultivation through reflection" would be lost;

however, by subsuming them under "cultivation through reflection," the specific names are still included. Thus, the traditional method is not lost, while the superior quality of comprehensive inclusion is maintained.

Therefore, one employs the cultivation of contemplation (*cintā-bhāvanā*) to distinguish it from [ordinary] dhyāna. Next, regarding the mutual interpenetration of the four dharmas: "interpenetration" means that each of the four names may be applied to dhyāna.

It is called *dhyāna* because it possesses the factors (*aṅga*). It is also called "concentration" (*samādhi*) because it is characterized by a single mind. It is also called "samādhi" because it is free from the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and crookedness.
It is also called a "pāramitā" because the five factors are perfected. This applies to all other concentrations, samādhis, and pāramitās as well.
It is also like this. If discussed separately, each has its own primary factor (*maula*); in the dhyānas, one possesses the factors (*aṅga*), and absorption (*samādhi*) proceeds from these factors.

In the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), there are both common factors and the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-aṅga*), which proceed from absorption. Thus, the *Yingluo jing* says: "Dhyāna is called a forest of factors; absorption is called the gathering of equanimity."
Samādhi follows the principle of conditions and is untainted, harmonious, and upright. The pāramitās take both phenomena and principle as their object, reaching the ultimate further shore.
To distinguish them individually so they do not become confused, dhyāna is called simply "dhyāna," while the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) are called simply "samādhi.
The *anāgamya* and *dhyānāntara* stages flank these two; because they depend on others for their designation, they are named "dhyāna. The *anāgamya* is about to arise, depending on its cause.

In the middle [stages], the fruit is explained; therefore, they receive the specific designation of "concentration" (*samādhi*). Because they have not yet taken the principle (*tattva*) as their object, they are not [yet] *samādhi*. Being incomplete, they are not *pāramitās*.

As for emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*), because they take only the principle as their object, although one enters the first dhyāna, one does not receive the name of its constituent factors (*aṅga*).

Even if it were called "dhyāna," it would be called only "pure dhyāna" (*śuddha-dhyāna*) and not "dhyāna of attachment" (*āsvāda-dhyāna*); it is merely "straightening" (*ṛju-karaṇa*) and is not called a constituent factor.

Although there is a fixed principle, this is precisely a matter of deeply savoring the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). It enters directly into the principle (*tattva*) without being named after that fixed state;
it has not yet reached the ultimate consummation of phenomena and principle, and thus is not called a *pāramitā*, a *pratisarga* (liberation), or the like.

While it arises from the four *dhyānas* and is both *dhyāna* and *samādhi*, because it is guided by a mind of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*), it is still not designated as a *samādhi*. It receives its superior name from the *pratisargas* and so forth.

The same applies to the meditative attainments of the formless realm (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Although they possess the three factors, they take up the state of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), for such immediacy truly depends upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

[As it is said: "With applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)," this refers to when the untainted (*anāsrava*) minds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*) enter the various dhyānas;

they are able to sever the crookedness of the sixty-two views and receive the name of *samādhi*, while other names are subsumed. [States such as] the resolve (*praṇidhāna*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and the summit (*mūrdhan*) are also dhyāna.
